name: The Vanishing Step
subject: Calculus I
source: OpenStax Calculus Volume 1 (CC BY); authored for Grimoire
blurb: Limits, derivatives and integrals - the mathematics of change.

relic.name: The Infinitesimal
relic.flavour: Awarded for clearing the Trial. Hints cost one less mana.

sections.title: Approaching Without Arriving
sections.body:
Every question calculus asks is really the same question: what happens to a quantity as something else closes in on a value it never reaches? The speed of a falling stone at an instant is an average speed over an interval of length zero; the slope of a curve at a point is a rise over a run of zero. Written down honestly both are $\frac{0}{0}$, which is not a number. The **limit** is the machinery that rescues these questions.

Take $f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$. At $x = 1$ it is genuinely undefined - there is a hole punched in the graph. But ask instead what $f$ does near $1$, and the answer is completely unambiguous: feed in $0.999$ and you get $1.999$, feed in $1.001$ and you get $2.001$. The output is closing in on $2$ from both sides, and nothing about the missing point interferes.

That is the whole idea. We write $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2$, and this says **nothing whatever about $f(1)$**. The definition deliberately excludes $x = a$, because the interesting cases are precisely the ones where the function is broken or undefined at the point in question. A limit that merely reported $f(a)$ would be a machine for telling you what you already knew.

So read $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ as: the values of $f$ can be forced as close to $L$ as anyone demands, by taking $x$ close enough to $a$ - but not equal to it. Three words carry the load: **forced**, **anyone**, and **not equal**.
sections.code:
f(x) = (x^2 - 1) / (x - 1)          domain: every real number EXCEPT x = 1

  x        0.9      0.99     0.999   |  1  |   1.001    1.01     1.1
  f(x)     1.9      1.99     1.999   | --- |   2.001    2.01     2.1

At x = 1 the formula reads 0/0, which is not a number, so f(1) does not exist.
Everywhere else the factorisation is legal:

      x^2 - 1       (x - 1)(x + 1)
     ---------  =  ----------------  =  x + 1        (for x =/= 1)
       x - 1            x - 1

So f agrees with the line y = x + 1 everywhere except at the single punched-out
point (1, 2).  The table closes in on 2 from both sides.

     lim   f(x)  =  2          while       f(1)  is undefined
    x->1

The limit is a statement about the NEIGHBOURHOOD of 1, never about 1 itself.

annotations.text: The excluded point is not an accident of this example - it is the normal situation. Derivatives are built entirely from functions undefined at the very point of interest.
Read the table outward-in from both ends. Approaching from below and from above must reach the same destination, or there is no limit at all.
The cancellation is legal because x is never equal to 1 - dividing by (x - 1) requires exactly that. This is why factoring solves 0/0 rather than cheating at it.
Say this out loud: the limit is 2, and f(1) does not exist. Both statements are true at once, and getting comfortable with that is most of the battle.

checkpoint.prompt: For $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$, fill in the two facts. Write the limit as a number, and write `undefined` for the value.
checkpoint.hint: One of these questions looks at the neighbourhood of 1; the other looks at 1 itself.
checkpoint.explain: The limit is $2$ because $f$ agrees with $x + 1$ at every point except $x = 1$, and $x + 1 \to 2$. The value $f(1)$ is undefined because substituting gives $\frac{0}{0}$. The tempting error is to declare the limit undefined too, on the grounds that the function is - but the limit never evaluates $f$ at the point.

sections.title: Two Roads In, and Three Ways to Fail
sections.body:
A point on the line can be approached from two directions, so a limit really has two halves. The **left-hand limit** $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)$ watches only $x < a$; the **right-hand limit** $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$ watches only $x > a$. The two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist **and agree**, and it then equals their common value. This is not a technicality - it is the definition split into its two obligations.

That gives a clean taxonomy of failure. The first way is the **jump**: both one-sided limits exist, but they are different numbers. The sign function $\frac{|x|}{x}$ is $-1$ to the left of $0$ and $+1$ to the right, so $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{|x|}{x}$ does not exist even though nothing is unbounded and nothing misbehaves.

The second is the **blow-up**: the values leave every bound. For $h(x) = \frac{1}{(x-2)^2}$ the output grows past any number you name, and we write $\lim_{x \to 2} h(x) = \infty$ as a description of how the limit fails, not as a claim that it exists. Note that $\frac{1}{x - 3}$ fails both ways at once: $-\infty$ on the left, $+\infty$ on the right.

The third is the strangest and the most instructive: **oscillation**. Take $k(x) = \sin(1/x)$ as $x \to 0$. Nothing is unbounded - $k$ stays inside $[-1, 1]$ forever - and there is no jump. But $1/x$ races to infinity, so $k$ runs through its entire range infinitely many times inside any window around $0$, however small. No candidate $L$ can be approached, because the function will always wander a full unit away again. Boundedness is not enough; settling is required.
sections.code:
ONE-SIDED               lim  f(x) = L  <=>  lim  f(x) = lim  f(x) = L
                       x->a                x->a-        x->a+

THE THREE FAILURES

(1) JUMP          g(x) = |x| / x        (2) BLOW-UP    h(x) = 1/(x - 2)^2

      lim  g(x) = -1                          lim  h(x) = +infinity
     x->0-                                   x->2
      lim  g(x) = +1                    the values leave every bound, so no
     x->0+                              finite L can be approached
    both sides exist, they disagree

(3) OSCILLATION   k(x) = sin(1/x)  as  x -> 0

      x = 1/pi     1/(2pi)   2/(5pi)   2/pi     as x shrinks, 1/x races to
      k(x) = 0       0         +1       +1      infinity and sin runs through
      x = 2/(3pi)  2/(7pi)                      its whole range infinitely
      k(x) = -1      -1                         often in ANY window round 0

    k never settles: it is bounded, yet no L is approached.

A subtler case: 1/(x - 3) has lim = -infinity on the left and +infinity on the
right, so it fails as a jump AND as a blow-up at once.

annotations.text: This biconditional is the workhorse. To show a limit does not exist, it is almost always cheapest to produce two disagreeing one-sided limits.
|x|/x is the standard jump. It is defined everywhere except 0, bounded, and perfectly well behaved on each side - none of which saves the limit.
Writing = +infinity is a description of the failure mode, not an existence claim. A limit equal to infinity does not exist as a number.
This is the sentence to remember about sin(1/x): infinitely many full oscillations inside every window around 0, no matter how narrow the window.

checkpoint.prompt: For $g(x) = \dfrac{|x|}{x}$, give the two one-sided limits at $0$ as signed numbers, then state whether the two-sided limit exists (`yes` or `no`).
checkpoint.template:
lim (x->0-) g(x) = ___
lim (x->0+) g(x) = ___
two-sided limit exists? ___
checkpoint.hint: For $x < 0$, $|x| = -x$. Substitute that in before deciding.
checkpoint.explain: To the left, $|x| = -x$, so $g(x) = -1$ identically; to the right $|x| = x$, so $g(x) = 1$. Both one-sided limits exist, so the failure is not caused by anything blowing up or oscillating - it is a pure jump, and disagreement alone is enough to destroy the two-sided limit.

sections.title: The Limit Laws and the 0/0 Loophole
sections.body:
Limits respect arithmetic. If $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M$ both exist, then the limit of a sum is $L + M$, of a product is $LM$, of a power is $L^n$, and of a quotient is $\frac{L}{M}$ - **provided $M \neq 0$**. Every one of these laws opens with the hypothesis that both limits exist, and the quotient law adds one more condition. Those conditions are where all the interesting problems live.

The immediate payoff is **direct substitution**. Because a polynomial is built from sums and products of $x$ and constants, $\lim_{x \to a} p(x) = p(a)$ for every polynomial, and the same holds for a rational function at any point where its denominator is not zero. For $\lim_{x \to 2}(3x^2 - 2x + 1)$ you simply substitute and get $9$.

When substitution produces $\frac{0}{0}$, the quotient law does not apply - it says nothing at all. That is what **indeterminate form** means: $\frac{0}{0}$ is not a value, and it is not a verdict of non-existence either. It is the algebra reporting that both parts vanish together, which is precisely the situation in which the answer could be anything. Compare $\frac{x^2}{x} \to 0$, $\frac{x}{x} \to 1$ and $\frac{x}{x^2} \to \infty$ at $0$: all three are $\frac{0}{0}$, and all three behave differently.

The cure is to rewrite the function so the vanishing factor cancels. **Factor** when the parts are polynomials: $\frac{x^2 - x - 6}{x - 3} = \frac{(x-3)(x+2)}{x-3} = x + 2 \to 5$. **Rationalise** when a root is present, by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate, so that $\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} \to \frac{1}{4}$. Both rewrites alter the function only at the single bad point - and the limit was never looking there.
sections.code:
LIMIT LAWS   (valid whenever  lim f = L  and  lim g = M  both exist)

   sum        lim (f + g) = L + M        power   lim f^n = L^n
   product    lim (f * g) = L * M        root    lim nth-root(f) = nth-root(L)
   quotient   lim (f / g) = L / M        ONLY IF  M =/= 0   <-- the whole story

Direct substitution therefore works for any polynomial, and for a rational
function wherever its denominator is not zero:

   lim (3x^2 - 2x + 1) = 3*(2)^2 - 2*(2) + 1 = 12 - 4 + 1 = 9
  x->2

WHEN SUBSTITUTION GIVES 0/0, THE QUOTIENT LAW IS SIMPLY SILENT.
0/0 is an INDETERMINATE FORM: it reports that numerator and denominator both
vanish, and nothing more.  Rewrite the function, then substitute.

  FACTOR          x^2 - x - 6      (x - 3)(x + 2)
                 -------------  =  --------------  =  x + 2  ->  5   as x -> 3
                    x - 3              x - 3

  RATIONALISE    sqrt(x + 4) - 2     sqrt(x+4) - 2   sqrt(x+4) + 2
                ----------------  =  ------------- * -------------
                       x                  x          sqrt(x+4) + 2

                      (x + 4) - 4              x                 1        1
                = -------------------- = --------------- = ------------- -> -
                   x (sqrt(x+4) + 2)     x (sqrt(x+4)+2)   sqrt(x+4)+2      4

Both rewrites change the function only at the one bad point - and the limit
never looked at that point anyway.

annotations.text: M =/= 0 is the condition that fails in every 0/0 problem you will meet. When it fails the law is silent - it does not report non-existence.
Direct substitution is a theorem about polynomials and rational functions, not a universal method. Always check what substitution actually returns before trusting it.
0/0 carries exactly one piece of information: both parts vanish at a. The answer can be any number, or infinity, or nothing at all.
Cancelling (x - 3) is only legal because x =/= 3 throughout the approach - which is exactly the hypothesis the limit hands you for free.
The conjugate works because (A - B)(A + B) = A^2 - B^2 kills the square root, moving the troublesome factor to where it can cancel.

checkpoint.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^3 - 1}{x - 1}$. Show the rewrite you used and say why it is legitimate.
checkpoint.explain: Substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$, so the quotient law is unavailable. Factoring gives $\frac{(x-1)(x^2+x+1)}{x-1} = x^2 + x + 1$, which is a polynomial, so substitution now applies and yields $1 + 1 + 1 = 3$. The common wrong answer is $1$, from cancelling the visible $x$ terms or from assuming $\frac{0}{0} = 1$.

sections.title: Trapping a Limit, and Saying It Precisely
sections.body:
Some functions defeat every law and every rewrite. $f(x) = x^2 \sin(1/x)$ near $0$ is a product of something tending to $0$ and something with no limit at all, so the product law cannot be invoked - its hypothesis is unmet. The way through is to stop computing and start **trapping**.

The **squeeze theorem** says: if $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ near $a$, and $g$ and $h$ both tend to the same $L$, then $f$ is forced to $L$ as well. It has nowhere else to go. Since $-1 \le \sin(1/x) \le 1$ for every $x \neq 0$, multiplying through by $x^2 \ge 0$ gives $-x^2 \le x^2\sin(1/x) \le x^2$; both wrappers tend to $0$, so the limit is $0$. Notice where the wildness went: it is still there, but it is confined.

Everything so far has leaned on the phrase close to, which is not yet mathematics. The precise definition turns it into a game. $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $0 < |x - a| < \delta$ implies $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$. A challenger names an output tolerance $\varepsilon$; you must answer with an input window $\delta$ that guarantees it. You must be able to answer every challenge, not merely a generous one.

Read the clause $0 < |x - a|$ once more - it is the punched-out point written in symbols, and it is why $f(a)$ is irrelevant. For $f(x) = 3x + 1$ at $a = 2$ with $L = 7$: $|(3x+1) - 7| = 3|x - 2|$, which is below $\varepsilon$ as soon as $|x - 2| < \varepsilon/3$, so $\delta = \varepsilon/3$ answers every challenge at once. You will not be drilled on this today. Recognise its shape, and notice that it says exactly what the tables and the pictures have been saying all along.
sections.code:
SQUEEZE THEOREM
   If  g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x)  near a (except possibly at a)
   and  lim g(x) = lim h(x) = L,   then  lim f(x) = L.
        x->a       x->a                  x->a

   f(x) = x^2 * sin(1/x)    sin(1/x) oscillates forever, so no law applies.
   But  -1 <= sin(1/x) <= 1  for every x =/= 0, so multiplying by x^2 >= 0:

            -x^2  <=  x^2 sin(1/x)  <=  x^2

            lim (-x^2) = 0     lim (x^2) = 0     =>   lim f(x) = 0
           x->0               x->0                   x->0

   The wrapper collapses onto 0 and drags the wild function with it.

THE PRECISE DEFINITION - read it once, slowly

   lim f(x) = L   means:   for every  epsilon > 0  there is a  delta > 0
  x->a                     such that  0 < |x - a| < delta  ==>  |f(x) - L| < eps

   epsilon      = the tolerance a challenger demands on the OUTPUT
   delta        = the closeness you supply on the INPUT
   0 < |x - a|  = the punched-out point: x = a is excluded, deliberately

   f(x) = 3x + 1,  a = 2,  L = 7:   |(3x + 1) - 7| = 3|x - 2| < eps
                                    whenever  |x - 2| < eps/3,  so delta = eps/3.

annotations.text: The bound -1 <= sin(anything) <= 1 holds for every input whatsoever, which is what makes it usable when the input is misbehaving.
Multiplying an inequality by x^2 preserves its direction because x^2 >= 0. Multiplying by x would not, and the argument would collapse.
epsilon comes first and is chosen by an adversary; delta comes second and is chosen by you in response. Swapping that order inverts the definition into something false.
0 < |x - a| excludes x = a. Every earlier remark that the limit ignores the point is this one inequality.
delta = eps/3 works for every eps at once, which is what the definition demands. A delta that only handles eps = 0.01 proves nothing.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the squeeze argument for $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \sin(1/x)$. Use `x^2` and `-x^2` for the wrappers and a number for the limits.
checkpoint.template:
___  <=  x^2 sin(1/x)  <=  ___
both wrappers tend to ___, so the limit is ___
checkpoint.hint: Start from $-1 \le \sin(1/x) \le 1$ and multiply through by $x^2$.
checkpoint.explain: The bound on $\sin$ holds for every argument, including one racing to infinity, so it survives where the product law does not. Multiplying by $x^2 \ge 0$ keeps the inequalities pointing the same way, and both wrappers collapse to $0$, leaving the trapped function no room. Concluding 'no limit, because $\sin(1/x)$ has none' is the tempting error - the factor $x^2$ crushes the oscillation.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the approach table for $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ as $x \to 1$. Give exact decimals, and write `undefined` where the function has no value.
guided-practice.hint: Away from $x = 1$ the function simplifies to $x + 1$.
guided-practice.explain: Every entry except the middle one is just $x + 1$, because the cancellation is valid whenever $x \neq 1$. The middle entry is undefined because substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$. The table therefore closes in on $2$ from both sides while stepping straight over a point that has no value at all - exactly the situation limits were invented to describe.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the steps for evaluating $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 - x - 6}{x - 3}$ into the correct order.
fragments: Substitute x = 3 and observe the indeterminate form 0/0.
Factor the numerator as (x - 3)(x + 2).
Cancel the factor (x - 3), which is legal because x is never equal to 3 on the approach.
Substitute x = 3 into the simplified expression x + 2.
Report the limit as 5.
guided-practice.hint: Nothing is rewritten until substitution has been tried and has failed.
guided-practice.explain: Substitution comes first because it is the cheapest test and, when the denominator does not vanish, it is the whole answer. Only after $\frac{0}{0}$ appears is a rewrite justified, and the cancellation must be defended by the fact that $x \neq 3$ throughout the approach. Rewriting before checking is how learners end up factoring problems that direct substitution would have finished in one line.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $f(x) = x + 1$ for $x < 2$ and $f(x) = x^2$ for $x \ge 2$. Find $\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x)$, then decide whether $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ exists. Justify the verdict.
guided-practice.answer: left 3, right 4, two-sided limit does not exist
guided-practice.hint: Each one-sided limit uses one branch of the definition and ignores the other entirely.
guided-practice.explain: Approaching from below only the branch $x + 1$ is in play, giving $3$; approaching from above only $x^2$ is in play, giving $4$. Both one-sided limits exist perfectly well, so the failure is a jump rather than a blow-up or an oscillation, and disagreement alone is enough to destroy it. The classic error is to answer $4$ because $f(2) = 4$ - but the value at the point never settles a limit.

guided-practice.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2}(3x^2 - 2x + 1)$ by the limit laws. Fill in the substituted values and the final answer as plain numbers.
guided-practice.explain: Direct substitution is legal here not by habit but by theorem: the sum, product and power laws applied to $\lim_{x \to 2} x = 2$ build the polynomial one operation at a time, so $\lim_{x \to a} p(x) = p(a)$. The arithmetic gives $12 - 4 + 1 = 9$. Substitution is only ever a shortcut for that chain of laws, which is why it stops working the moment a law's hypothesis fails.

guided-practice.prompt: Name the three distinct ways a limit can fail to exist, give the standard example of each, and say what distinguishes the third from the other two.
guided-practice.hint: One example is bounded and settles on each side, one is unbounded, and one is bounded but never settles.
guided-practice.explain: A jump has two one-sided limits that both exist and disagree, as with $\frac{|x|}{x}$ at $0$. A blow-up leaves every bound, as with $\frac{1}{(x-2)^2}$ at $2$. Oscillation is the instructive one: $\sin(1/x)$ at $0$ stays inside $[-1, 1]$ and has no jump, yet crosses its whole range infinitely often in every window, so boundedness plainly does not imply that a limit exists.

limit-workshop.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^2 + 3x}{x^2 - 9}$, or show that it fails to exist. Factor first, then say exactly what substitution returns after the rewrite.
limit-workshop.answer: does not exist; the one-sided limits are -infinity and +infinity
limit-workshop.hint: Factor both parts, then look carefully at what actually cancels - and at what does not.
limit-workshop.explain: Factoring gives $\frac{x(x+3)}{(x-3)(x+3)} = \frac{x}{x-3}$ for $x \neq -3$, so the cancellation removes the trouble at $-3$ and leaves the trouble at $3$ completely untouched. Substituting now gives $\frac{3}{0}$, not $\frac{0}{0}$: the numerator does not vanish, so this is a blow-up, negative from the left and positive from the right, and the limit does not exist. The trap is assuming every factorisation ends in a finite answer - the same algebra gives the limit $\frac{1}{2}$ at $-3$ and nothing at all at $3$.

Substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$, and no factorisation is visible while a root sits inside a difference. Multiplying by $\frac{\sqrt{x+9}+3}{\sqrt{x+9}+3}$ turns the numerator into $(x + 9) - 9 = x$, which cancels the $x$ below and leaves $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+9}+3} \to \frac{1}{6}$. Answering $\frac{1}{3}$ is the standard slip - it comes from stopping before the surviving denominator is evaluated.

limit-workshop.prompt: Suppose $4x - 9 \le f(x) \le x^2 - 4x + 7$ for all $x \ge 0$. Find $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)$, name the theorem that licenses the conclusion, and say what would happen to the argument if the two bounds disagreed at $4$.
limit-workshop.hint: Evaluate both bounding functions at $x = 4$ before doing anything else.
limit-workshop.explain: Both wrappers are polynomials, so substitution gives $4(4) - 9 = 7$ and $16 - 16 + 7 = 7$. Because they agree, $f$ is pinned between two quantities heading to the same place and the squeeze theorem forces $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 7$ - even though no formula for $f$ was ever supplied. Had the bounds disagreed, the theorem would say nothing whatever, which is why checking that they match is the actual work rather than a formality.

limit-workshop.prompt: Classify how the limit fails in each case, using exactly one of jump, blow-up or oscillation: (a) $\dfrac{|x|}{x}$ at $0$; (b) $\dfrac{1}{(x-2)^2}$ at $2$; (c) $\sin(1/x)$ at $0$. Justify each classification with the one-sided behaviour.
limit-workshop.hint: Ask of each: are the values bounded, and do they settle on each side?
limit-workshop.explain: In (a) both sides settle, at $-1$ and $+1$, and merely disagree - a jump. In (b) the values are positive and unbounded on both sides, so it is a blow-up and we write $+\infty$ to describe the failure. In (c) the values never leave $[-1, 1]$, so nothing is unbounded, yet $1/x$ races to infinity and $\sin(1/x)$ completes infinitely many oscillations in every window around $0$; calling this a jump is the common error, but there is no one-sided limit here to jump between.

limit-workshop.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{2 - x}{x^2 - 4}$, and explain precisely which hypothesis of the quotient law fails and what you did instead.
limit-workshop.explain: The quotient law requires the denominator's limit to be non-zero, and here it is $0$, so the law is inapplicable rather than false. Writing $2 - x = -(x-2)$ and factoring below gives $\frac{-(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+2)} = \frac{-1}{x+2} \to -\frac{1}{4}$. Losing the minus sign and answering $\frac{1}{4}$ is the standard casualty here - the numerator is $2 - x$, not $x - 2$.

exam.prompt: Which statement is the definition of $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$?
choices: The values of $f(x)$ can be made as close to $L$ as desired by taking $x$ sufficiently close to, but not equal to, $a$.
$f(x)$ eventually equals $L$ for some $x$ near $a$.
$f$ is defined at $a$ and its graph has no break there.
exam.explain: The limit is a statement about arbitrary closeness on a punctured neighbourhood, which is why the phrase 'but not equal to' cannot be dropped. Option B is the seductive one - it holds for continuous functions and fails for exactly the functions limits were built to handle, such as $\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}$ at $1$, whose limit is $2$ although $f(1)$ does not exist.

exam.prompt: Which is a correct statement of the squeeze theorem?
choices: If $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ near $a$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$.
If $g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)$ near $a$ and both $g$ and $h$ have limits at $a$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists.
If $f$ is bounded near $a$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists.
If $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = L$ and $g(x) \le f(x)$ near $a$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists and is at least $L$.
exam.explain: The wrappers must converge to the same value; that equality is the whole mechanism, since it is what leaves the trapped function nowhere to go. Option B drops it and is false - $-1 \le \sin(1/x) \le 1$ has convergent bounds and no limit. Option C is refuted by the same example, and option D supplies only a one-sided bound, which never establishes existence.

exam.prompt: Give the one-sided limits of $h(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 3}$ at $3$, using `-infinity` or `+infinity`, then state whether $\lim_{x \to 3} h(x)$ exists (`yes` or `no`).
exam.template:
lim (x->3-) h(x) = ___
lim (x->3+) h(x) = ___
two-sided limit exists? ___
exam.hint: Just below $3$ the denominator is a small negative number.
exam.explain: For $x$ slightly below $3$ the denominator is small and negative, driving the quotient to $-\infty$; just above, it is small and positive, giving $+\infty$. Unlike $\frac{1}{(x-3)^2}$, which is $+\infty$ from both sides, this function fails as a blow-up and as a disagreement at once - so not even the description $\lim = \infty$ is available.

exam.prompt: For $f(x) = 3x + 1$, $a = 2$ and $L = 7$: find a $\delta$ that works for $\varepsilon = 0.06$, then give a $\delta$ in terms of $\varepsilon$ that answers every challenge. Show the algebra connecting them.
exam.answer: delta = epsilon/3, so delta = 0.02
exam.hint: Simplify $|(3x+1) - 7|$ first; it collapses to a multiple of $|x - 2|$.
exam.explain: The output error is $|(3x+1) - 7| = |3x - 6| = 3|x-2|$, so demanding it below $\varepsilon$ is exactly demanding $|x - 2| < \varepsilon/3$; with $\varepsilon = 0.06$ that is $\delta = 0.02$. The point of the second half is that one formula answers every challenge at once - producing only the numerical $\delta$ proves nothing, because the definition quantifies over all $\varepsilon > 0$ before $\delta$ is ever chosen.

exam.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{x - 4}{\sqrt{x} - 2}$. Show your rewrite.
exam.hint: Either multiply by the conjugate $\sqrt{x} + 2$, or notice that $x - 4$ is a difference of two squares in $\sqrt{x}$.
exam.explain: Substitution gives $\frac{0}{0}$. Multiplying by $\frac{\sqrt{x}+2}{\sqrt{x}+2}$ makes the denominator $x - 4$, which cancels the numerator and leaves $\sqrt{x} + 2 \to 4$; equivalently $x - 4 = (\sqrt{x}-2)(\sqrt{x}+2)$ directly. Answering $1$ - as though $\frac{0}{0}$ were $1$, or as though the two $x - 4$ expressions simply cancelled - is the failure this problem is built to expose.

exam.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{3}}{x - 3}$. Show how you cleared the inner fractions.
exam.hint: Combine the numerator over the common denominator $3x$ before touching anything else.
exam.explain: The numerator is $\frac{3 - x}{3x}$, so the whole expression is $\frac{3-x}{3x(x-3)} = \frac{-1}{3x} \to -\frac{1}{9}$. Both traps are about sign and order: $3 - x = -(x - 3)$ is what produces the minus, and answering $\frac{1}{9}$ means that negation was dropped somewhere. A complex fraction is always cleared from the inside outwards.

exam.prompt: A student writes: 'Since $f(x) = \frac{x^2-1}{x-1}$ is undefined at $x = 1$, the limit there is undefined too.' Explain what is wrong with the reasoning, and describe what the graph actually looks like near $x = 1$.
exam.hint: Which point does the definition of the limit deliberately exclude?
exam.explain: The definition examines $0 < |x - 1| < \delta$, a punctured neighbourhood, so the value at the point is excluded by construction and cannot decide anything. The graph is the line $y = x + 1$ with a single hole at $(1, 2)$, and the limit is $2$ precisely because every nearby value is near $2$. The student's rule would make limits useless, since every derivative is a limit of a quotient undefined at exactly the point of interest.

exam.prompt: Put the steps for evaluating $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x+4} - 2}{x}$ into the correct order.
fragments: Substitute x = 0 and obtain the indeterminate form 0/0.
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate sqrt(x+4) + 2.
Simplify the numerator to (x + 4) - 4 = x.
Cancel the factor x, valid because x is never 0 on the approach.
Substitute into 1/(sqrt(x+4) + 2) to get 1/4.
exam.explain: The conjugate is applied only after substitution has produced $\frac{0}{0}$, and its purpose is to convert the difference of roots into $(x+4) - 4$ so that a factor of $x$ appears where it can cancel. Cancelling before simplifying the numerator is impossible, because no common factor exists until the difference of squares has been carried out.

exam.prompt: Tabulate $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$ at the values below to watch the limit at $3$ emerge. Give each value as an exact decimal, and the limit as a whole number.
exam.hint: For $x \neq 3$ the function is simply $x + 3$.
exam.explain: Factoring gives $\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3} = x + 3$ away from $3$, so each tabulated value is just $x + 3$ and the column converges on $6$ from both sides. Tables build intuition but never prove a limit: $\sin(1/x)$ sampled at $x = \frac{1}{n\pi}$ produces a flawless column of zeros for a limit that does not exist.

exam.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} x \cos(1/x)$, or show it does not exist. Name the theorem you use and state the bounds explicitly.
exam.hint: Bound $\cos(1/x)$ first, then multiply by $|x|$ rather than by $x$.
exam.explain: Because $-1 \le \cos(1/x) \le 1$ for every $x \neq 0$, we get $-|x| \le x\cos(1/x) \le |x|$, and both wrappers tend to $0$, so the squeeze theorem gives $0$. Multiplying the inequality by $x$ rather than $|x|$ is the trap: for negative $x$ that reverses the inequalities and the sandwich falls apart. Declaring the limit non-existent because $\cos(1/x)$ has none misapplies the product law, whose hypothesis - that both factors have limits - is unmet.

sections.title: The Three-Part Condition
sections.body:
A limit deliberately ignores the point it is aimed at. The value of $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ is decided entirely by what $f$ does **near** $a$ and never by $f(a)$ itself - that was the whole purpose of the deleted neighbourhood. **Continuity** is the extra demand that the point and its neighbourhood finally agree.

A function $f$ is **continuous at $a$** when three things hold: $f(a)$ is defined; $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists; and $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$. Compressed into one sentence, continuity at $a$ says exactly this: **the limit may be computed by substitution**. Every limit you have ever evaluated by plugging the number in was a use of continuity you had not yet been told about.

The three clauses look redundant, and they are not. Each can fail while the other two survive - $(x^2-4)/(x-2)$ has a limit at $2$ and no value there; $|x|/x$ has neither at $0$; a function pinned to a stray value at one point has both and they disagree. No two of the clauses imply the third, which is why the definition is a list rather than a slogan.

Continuity **on an open interval** $(a,b)$ means continuity at every point of it. At the endpoint of a closed interval $[a,b]$ only one side of the point exists, so we ask only for $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) = f(b)$ - **one-sided continuity**. Without that concession $\sqrt{x}$ would count as discontinuous at $0$ merely because the left half of the picture is not there to be checked.
sections.code:
CONTINUOUS AT a  requires all three, and in this order:

   (1)  f(a) is defined         the point is there at all
   (2)  lim f(x)  exists        the neighbourhood agrees with itself
        x->a
   (3)  lim f(x) = f(a)         point and neighbourhood agree
        x->a

Each one can fail while the other two survive:

   f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2)            at a = 2
        f(2) = 0/0 is UNDEFINED           -> (1) fails
        the limit is 4, so (2) is fine

   f(x) = |x| / x                      at a = 0
        one-sided limits are -1 and +1    -> (2) fails
        there is no single limit for anything to be compared with

   f(x) = { x^2   for x =/= 1
          {  5    for x  =  1          at a = 1
        f(1) = 5 exists, the limit is 1, and 5 =/= 1
        -> (3) fails: both halves exist and simply disagree

AT AN ENDPOINT ONLY ONE SIDE EXISTS

   sqrt(x) on [0, oo):     lim   sqrt(x) = 0 = sqrt(0)
                          x->0+

   so sqrt is continuous FROM THE RIGHT at 0, and that is all we ask of
   an endpoint. Otherwise no function on a closed interval could ever be
   called continuous, and the theorems that need [a, b] would be empty.

annotations.text: Clause (3) is the one that does the work: it is what licenses substitution. Clauses (1) and (2) exist only so that (3) has two sides to compare.
A two-sided limit exists only when both sides agree. Here they disagree by a fixed amount, so no repair at the single point x = 0 can help.
This is the case people forget exists. The function is defined, the limit exists, and it is still discontinuous - because nobody made them equal.
One-sided continuity at an endpoint is a genuine weakening of the definition, adopted because the alternative is useless, not because it is a technicality.

checkpoint.prompt: Take $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$ at $a = 2$. Fill each blank exactly as instructed.
checkpoint.template:
f(2) is ___                       (write defined or undefined)
the limit as x -> 2 is ___         (a number)
the first condition to fail is number ___
checkpoint.explain: Substituting $2$ gives $0/0$, so $f(2)$ does not exist and clause $(1)$ fails immediately. The limit is unaffected: cancelling the common factor leaves $x+2 \to 4$, because a limit never asks about $x = 2$ itself. The tempting answer for the second blank is **does not exist** - but a missing value and a missing limit are different failures, and confusing them is the commonest error on this floor.

sections.title: Three Ways the Condition Fails
sections.body:
A discontinuity is not one phenomenon, and the classification is far more useful than the bare word. A **removable** discontinuity is one where $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ exists but $f(a)$ is missing or is some other number: the graph has a **hole**, and defining $f(a) = L$ repairs it in one stroke.

A **jump** discontinuity has both one-sided limits finite but different. Nothing repairs it, because whatever value you assign to $f(a)$ disagrees with at least one side - and altering a function at a single point never moves a limit anyway. The size of the jump, $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f - \lim_{x \to a^-} f$, is a genuine measurement, which is why step functions and tax bands live here.

An **infinite** discontinuity has at least one one-sided limit equal to $+\infty$ or $-\infty$, and the line $x = a$ is then a **vertical asymptote**. Since $\infty$ is not a value, this is really clause $(2)$ failing - the limit does not exist - dressed in more informative language.

For a rational function the whole classification is settled by factoring. A denominator zero whose factor **cancels** leaves a hole; one that **survives** leaves an asymptote. A zero denominator on its own tells you which points to examine and nothing whatever about which species you have found.
sections.code:
f(x) = (x^2 - x - 6)/(x^2 - 9)  =  ((x - 3)(x + 2)) / ((x - 3)(x + 3))

Two bad points, and they are NOT the same kind of bad.

  x = 3     the factor (x - 3) cancels
            lim  f(x) = lim (x + 2)/(x + 3) = 5/6      finite
            x->3
            f(3) is undefined       ->  REMOVABLE
            patch it: define f(3) = 5/6 and f is continuous there

  x = -3    the factor (x + 3) does NOT cancel
            numerator -> 6, denominator -> 0
            lim   f(x) = +oo        lim   f(x) = -oo
            x->-3-                  x->-3+
            ->  INFINITE, a vertical asymptote at x = -3
            no value assigned to f(-3) can ever repair this

THE THIRD SPECIES IS A JUMP

  f(x) = { 2x + 1   for x <  1
         { x^2 + 3  for x >= 1

            left limit = 3      right limit = 4      both finite
            3 =/= 4   ->  JUMP, of size 1
            f(1) = 4, so f is continuous from the right at 1 and is
            nowhere near continuous from the left

THE TEST IS THE CANCELLING, NOT THE ZERO DENOMINATOR

  a factor that cancels  -> hole      (removable)
  a factor that survives -> asymptote (infinite)

Three species is not a complete list for every function - sin(1/x) at
x = 0 oscillates too fast to be any of them - but it is complete for
every rational and piecewise function on this floor.

annotations.text: Removable does not mean harmless - f really is discontinuous at 3 as written. It means one edit at one point fixes it, which is untrue of the other two species.
The two sides run to opposite infinities because (x + 3) changes sign at -3 while the numerator does not. Odd-order surviving factors flip; even-order ones do not.
Both one-sided limits exist and are finite. That is exactly what separates a jump from an infinite discontinuity, and it is the only thing that does.
Read this line before answering any classification question. Anyone who hunts only for zeros of the denominator calls every one of them an asymptote, and is wrong about half of them.

checkpoint.prompt: Classify each discontinuity. Give the first answer as a number, and each of the others as one of `removable`, `jump` or `infinite`.

steps.label: kind of discontinuity of (x^3 - 1)/(x - 1) at x = 1
kind of discontinuity of 1/(x - 1)^2 at x = 1
kind of discontinuity of |x|/x at x = 0

checkpoint.explain: $x^3 - 1 = (x-1)(x^2+x+1)$, so the offending factor cancels and the limit is $1 + 1 + 1 = 3$: a hole, repaired by setting $f(1) = 3$. In $1/(x-1)^2$ nothing cancels and the limit is $+\infty$ from both sides - an even power, so no sign flip. And $|x|/x$ is $-1$ left of $0$ and $+1$ right of it: two finite disagreeing limits, a jump of size $2$, and not - despite the fraction - anything infinite.

sections.title: Built Continuous, Then Trusted
sections.body:
Almost nothing is proved continuous from the definition twice. Constants and $x$ are continuous; sums, products and quotients of continuous functions are continuous wherever the denominator is non-zero; and a composition $f(g(x))$ is continuous at $a$ whenever $g$ is continuous at $a$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(a)$. Everything else is assembled from those.

Two consequences carry most of the weight. **Every polynomial is continuous on all of $\mathbb{R}$**, and **every rational function is continuous exactly on its domain** - so the only candidate discontinuities of $p(x)/q(x)$ sit at zeros of $q$, and nowhere else at all. Composition extends the same convenience to $\sqrt{x^2-4}$ or $\cos(x^3)$, where the trouble is located by inspecting the inside function.

This matters because continuity is the hypothesis of the first genuinely powerful theorem in the subject. The **Intermediate Value Theorem** says that if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $N$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(c) = N$ for at least one $c$ in $(a,b)$: a continuous function cannot get from one value to another without passing through everything in between.

The honest use is **root bracketing**. Take $N = 0$, so that opposite signs at the endpoints guarantee a root inside; then halve the interval while preserving the sign change and the root is located to any accuracy you like. What the theorem never supplies is uniqueness, a formula, or a position - and it collapses entirely if continuity fails anywhere in $[a,b]$, which is how $1/x$ manages to run from $-1$ to $1$ on $[-1,1]$ without ever being zero.
sections.code:
BUILDING BLOCKS

  constants and x            continuous on all of R
  sums and products          continuous wherever the pieces are
  quotients                  continuous wherever the denominator =/= 0
  compositions               f(g(x)) is continuous at a whenever g is
                             continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a)

  => every polynomial is continuous on (-oo, oo)
  => every rational function is continuous exactly on its own domain
  => sqrt(x^2 - 4) is continuous on (-oo, -2] and on [2, oo)

INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM

  f continuous on the CLOSED interval [a, b], and N lying between
  f(a) and f(b)
    ==>  there is at least one c in (a, b) with f(c) = N.

ROOT BRACKETING is the case N = 0: a SIGN CHANGE guarantees a root.

  g(x) = x^3 - x - 1  is a polynomial, hence continuous on [1, 2]

     g(1) = -1 < 0        g(2) = 5 > 0        sign change
     ==> a root exists somewhere in (1, 2)

  Halve the bracket, keeping whichever half still changes sign:

     g(3/2)  =    7/8  > 0   ->  root in (1, 3/2)
     g(5/4)  = -19/64  < 0   ->  root in (5/4, 3/2)
     g(11/8) = 115/512 > 0   ->  root in (5/4, 11/8)

  The true root is 1.3247179...; three halvings have pinned it inside a
  bracket of width 1/8 without solving a cubic at all.

WHAT THE THEOREM DOES NOT SAY

  not unique     f may hit the value N many times over
  not located    it names no c, only an interval that contains one
  not optional   on [-1, 1], f(x) = 1/x runs from -1 up to 1 and is
                 never 0 - it is discontinuous at 0, so the theorem
                 was never available in the first place

annotations.text: This one line saves most of the work on the floor: to find a rational function's discontinuities, factor the denominator and look nowhere else.
Closed, and continuous at every point of it. One bad point anywhere inside voids the conclusion outright rather than merely weakening it.
The sign change is the entire input. The size of the values is irrelevant: -0.001 and +0.001 would prove precisely as much.
IVT is an existence theorem and nothing more. Reading it as 'there is exactly one root' is the standard overclaim, and x^3 - x has three roots in [-2, 2] to disprove it.

checkpoint.prompt: Let $p(x) = x^3 - 4x + 1$. Show that $p$ has a root in $(0,1)$, naming the hypothesis of the Intermediate Value Theorem you rely on, then perform one bisection step to halve the bracket. State what you have and have not established about the number of roots.
checkpoint.answer: p is a polynomial, so it is continuous on the closed interval [0, 1]. p(0) = 1 > 0 and p(1) = 1 - 4 + 1 = -2 < 0, so 0 lies between p(0) and p(1) and the Intermediate Value Theorem supplies a c in (0,1) with p(c) = 0. Bisecting: p(1/2) = 1/8 - 2 + 1 = -7/8 < 0, so the sign change now sits between 0 and 1/2 and the root lies in (0, 1/2). This establishes that at least one root exists there; it establishes nothing about uniqueness, and indeed p(2) = 1 > 0, so a second root lies in (1, 2).
checkpoint.explain: $p(0) = 1$ and $p(1) = -2$ have opposite signs, and $p$ is a polynomial so continuity on $[0,1]$ comes for free - that is the hypothesis, and it is the only one. The midpoint value $p(1/2) = -7/8$ is negative, so the sign change now lies between $0$ and $1/2$ and the bracket halves to $(0, 1/2)$. The overclaim to avoid is **therefore the root is unique**: $p(2) = 1$ is positive again, so there is a second root in $(1,2)$ that this argument knew nothing about.

sections.title: Behaviour at the Ends
sections.body:
$\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L$ means $f(x)$ can be forced as close to $L$ as you please by taking $x$ large enough. Nothing about it is a limit **at a point**: $\infty$ is a direction rather than a place, there is no $f(\infty)$, and the three-part condition has nothing to say. When such a limit exists, the line $y = L$ is a **horizontal asymptote** of the graph.

One fact drives every computation: $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{x^k} = 0$ for every $k > 0$. Dividing the numerator and denominator of a rational function by the highest power appearing in the **denominator** turns every remaining term into some $1/x^k$, and the answer falls out.

That yields a trichotomy worth memorising. If $\deg p < \deg q$ then $p/q \to 0$; if $\deg p = \deg q$ the limit is the ratio of the **leading coefficients**; if $\deg p > \deg q$ the quotient runs off to $\pm\infty$ and there is no horizontal asymptote at all. The constant terms never matter - end behaviour is decided by the largest powers alone.

Two warnings. Square roots flip sign: $\sqrt{x^2} = |x| = -x$ when $x < 0$, so $\sqrt{4x^2+1}/(3x-5) \to 2/3$ as $x \to \infty$ but $\to -2/3$ as $x \to -\infty$, giving **two** horizontal asymptotes rather than one. And a graph may cross its horizontal asymptote as often as it likes, because the definition constrains the tail and never the middle.
sections.code:
lim   f(x) = L   means f(x) can be forced as close to L as you like by
x->oo            taking x large enough. "oo" is a DIRECTION, not a place,
                 so there is no f(oo) to compare anything with and no
                 three-part condition to check here.

                 y = L is then a HORIZONTAL ASYMPTOTE of the graph.

EVERYTHING RESTS ON ONE FACT:     lim  1/x^k = 0    for every k > 0
                                 x->oo

RATIONAL FUNCTIONS: divide top and bottom by the largest power below.

  (3x^2 - 5x + 1)/(2x^2 + 7)     divide through by x^2
      = (3 - 5/x + 1/x^2)/(2 + 7/x^2)  ->  3/2      HA:  y = 3/2

  (2x + 1)/(x^2 - 3)             bottom wins   ->  0      HA:  y = 0

  (x^3 + 1)/(4x^2 - x)           top wins      ->  +oo    NO horizontal
                                                          asymptote

  degree top  <  degree bottom   ->  y = 0
  degree top  =  degree bottom   ->  y = (leading top)/(leading bottom)
  degree top  >  degree bottom   ->  no horizontal asymptote at all

ROOTS FLIP SIGNS:   sqrt(x^2) = |x|,   which is -x when x < 0.

  sqrt(4x^2 + 1)/(3x - 5)   ->   2/3   as x -> +oo
                            ->  -2/3   as x -> -oo

Two horizontal asymptotes, and the minus sign is not a slip: a square
root is never negative, so for very negative x the top stays positive
while the bottom has gone negative.

A graph is also perfectly free to CROSS its horizontal asymptote - the
definition constrains the tail, not the middle.

annotations.text: This is why 'continuous at infinity' is a meaningless phrase. A limit at infinity describes a tail; continuity describes a point.
Below, meaning in the denominator. Dividing by the largest power found anywhere is the usual slip, and it turns a finite answer into 0 or into an unresolved infinity.
No horizontal asymptote does not mean no end behaviour. When the top wins by exactly one degree there is a slant asymptote instead, which later floors will use.
Whenever a square root of an even power appears, test one large negative number such as x = -1000. It costs ten seconds and catches the commonest error in the section.

checkpoint.prompt: Evaluate each limit as $x \to \infty$, then count asymptotes. Write fractions like `2/3`, and whole numbers as whole numbers.
checkpoint.template:
lim (7x^2 + 3)/(2 - x^2)   = ___
lim (x^2 + 1)/(x^3 - 2)    = ___
number of horizontal asymptotes of (5x - 2)/sqrt(9x^2 + 4): ___
checkpoint.explain: Equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients, $7/(-1) = -7$; the leading coefficient of $2 - x^2$ is $-1$, and reading it as $2$ is what produces the wrong answer $7/2$. In the second the denominator wins outright, so the limit is $0$. The third has $\sqrt{9x^2+4} = |x|\sqrt{9 + 4/x^2}$, giving $5/3$ as $x \to \infty$ and $-5/3$ as $x \to -\infty$: two distinct horizontal asymptotes.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $g(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$. Answer for the point $a = 3$, writing `defined` or `undefined`, then a number, then one of `removable`, `jump`, `infinite`.
guided-practice.template:
g(3) is ___
the limit as x -> 3 is ___
the discontinuity at x = 3 is ___
the value that would repair it is ___
guided-practice.hint: Factor the numerator as $(x-3)(x+3)$ before doing anything else.
guided-practice.explain: $g(3)$ is $0/0$, so clause $(1)$ fails and $g$ is genuinely discontinuous there. But the factor $(x-3)$ cancels, leaving $x + 3 \to 6$, so the limit exists and the hole can be filled by declaring $g(3) = 6$. The tempting wrong answer is **infinite**, on the grounds that the denominator hits zero; a zero denominator only tells you where to look, and the cancelling tells you what you have found.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the classification procedure for a discontinuity of $f$ at $x = a$ into working order.
fragments: Compute the two one-sided limits of f as x -> a- and as x -> a+.
If either one-sided limit is infinite, stop: the discontinuity is infinite and x = a is a vertical asymptote.
Otherwise both one-sided limits are finite; if they differ, stop: the discontinuity is a jump, of size equal to their difference.
Otherwise they agree, so the two-sided limit L exists; now look at the value f(a).
If f(a) is undefined or differs from L, the discontinuity is removable, and redefining f(a) = L repairs it.
guided-practice.explain: The one-sided limits come first because every later question is asked about them - which species you have depends on whether they are infinite, whether they differ, and only lastly on $f(a)$. Checking $f(a)$ early is the natural instinct and it is wasted work: the value is irrelevant unless the two sides have already agreed on a finite $L$.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 - 3x + 2}$. Factor it, classify the behaviour at every point where the denominator vanishes, give the intervals on which $f$ is continuous, and state its horizontal asymptote.
guided-practice.answer: Factoring gives f(x) = (x-1)(x+1) / ((x-1)(x-2)) = (x+1)/(x-2) for x =/= 1. At x = 1 the factor cancels, so the limit is (1+1)/(1-2) = -2 and the discontinuity is removable; defining f(1) = -2 repairs it. At x = 2 the factor (x-2) survives and the numerator tends to 3, so the limits are -infinity from the left and +infinity from the right: an infinite discontinuity with a vertical asymptote x = 2. As a quotient of polynomials, f is continuous exactly on its domain, namely (-infinity, 1), (1, 2) and (2, infinity). Numerator and denominator both have degree 2 with leading coefficients 1 and 1, so the horizontal asymptote is y = 1.
guided-practice.hint: $x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x-1)(x-2)$. One of those factors meets a matching factor upstairs and one does not.
guided-practice.explain: Both denominator zeros look identical until you factor: $(x-1)$ cancels and $(x-2)$ does not, so $x = 1$ is a hole at height $-2$ while $x = 2$ is a vertical asymptote. Note the hole sits at $y = -2$, not at $y = 0$ - a removable discontinuity has a perfectly ordinary height, and reporting the hole as being 'at zero' is a frequent slip. The horizontal asymptote is $y = 1$ from equal degrees, and it is genuinely unrelated to the vertical one.

guided-practice.prompt: Find the value of $c$ making $$f(x) = \begin{cases} cx + 2 & x < 3 \\ x^2 - c & x \ge 3 \end{cases}$$ continuous at $x = 3$. Set out the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value $f(3)$, and say which of the three clauses of continuity each equality enforces.
guided-practice.answer: The left-hand limit is lim as x -> 3- of (cx + 2) = 3c + 2, since cx + 2 is a polynomial and hence continuous. The right-hand limit is lim as x -> 3+ of (x^2 - c) = 9 - c, and f(3) = 9 - c as well because the second piece is the one that owns x = 3. Clause (1) holds automatically. Clause (2), existence of the two-sided limit, requires the left and right limits to be equal: 3c + 2 = 9 - c, so 4c = 7 and c = 7/4. Clause (3) is then free, since the common limit 3(7/4) + 2 = 29/4 already equals f(3) = 9 - 7/4 = 29/4. So c = 7/4.
guided-practice.hint: Each piece is a polynomial, so each one-sided limit is found by substituting $x = 3$ into that piece.
guided-practice.explain: Each branch is a polynomial, so its one-sided limit is just substitution: $3c+2$ from the left, $9-c$ from the right. Continuity forces $3c + 2 = 9 - c$, hence $c = 7/4$ and a common value of $29/4$. The famous wrong move is to equate the two formulas at some other point, or to solve only $f(3) = $ the left limit while forgetting that $f(3)$ comes from the branch containing $x = 3$; here the $\ge$ decides that the right-hand branch owns the point.

guided-practice.prompt: Evaluate each limit as $x \to \infty$. Write fractions as `3/2`, whole numbers plainly, and for the last row write `none` if there is no horizontal asymptote.
guided-practice.hint: Compare the degrees first; only when they are equal do the coefficients matter.
guided-practice.explain: Equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients: $3/2$ in the first, and $-1/3$ in the third, where the numerator's leading coefficient is $-1$ and the visible $1$ is a decoy. In the second the denominator outranks the numerator, so the quotient is squeezed to $0$. In the fourth the numerator wins and the quotient runs to $+\infty$, so there is no horizontal asymptote - answering $\infty$ names the limit but not an asymptote, since a horizontal asymptote must be a real number $L$.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Let $h(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{x^2 + 2x - 3}$. Classify the behaviour at both zeros of the denominator, give the exact intervals of continuity, and find the horizontal asymptote. Explain why the horizontal asymptote is **not** the ratio of the leading coefficients here.
continuity-workshop.answer: x^2 + 2x - 3 = (x + 3)(x - 1), so h(x) = 1/(x - 1) for x =/= -3. At x = -3 the factor cancels: the limit is 1/(-3 - 1) = -1/4, so the discontinuity is removable and defining h(-3) = -1/4 repairs it. At x = 1 nothing cancels, the numerator tends to 4, and the one-sided limits are -infinity from the left and +infinity from the right: an infinite discontinuity with the vertical asymptote x = 1. As a rational function h is continuous exactly on its domain: (-infinity, -3), (-3, 1) and (1, infinity). The horizontal asymptote is y = 0, because the degree of the numerator, 1, is strictly less than the degree of the denominator, 2. The ratio-of-leading-coefficients rule applies only when the degrees are equal, so it has no bearing here.
continuity-workshop.hint: Factor the denominator first. Then compare degrees on the **original** expression before quoting any asymptote rule.
continuity-workshop.explain: The numerator $x+3$ is one of the denominator's factors, so $x = -3$ is a hole at height $-1/4$ while $x = 1$ is a vertical asymptote. The intervals of continuity omit both points, because a removable discontinuity is still a discontinuity until somebody actually redefines the function. The horizontal asymptote is $y = 0$ by degree comparison; quoting $1/1$ from the surviving form $1/(x-1)$, or $1/1$ from the visible leading coefficients, both produce the wrong answer $y = 1$.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Let $q(x) = x^5 + x - 1$. Bracket a root of $q$ in $[0,1]$ using the Intermediate Value Theorem, then bisect twice, showing the exact value of $q$ at each midpoint and the surviving bracket after each step.
continuity-workshop.answer: q is a polynomial and so is continuous on the closed interval [0, 1]. q(0) = -1 < 0 and q(1) = 1 > 0, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem with N = 0 there is a c in (0, 1) with q(c) = 0. First bisection: q(1/2) = 1/32 + 1/2 - 1 = -15/32 < 0, matching the sign at 0, so the sign change now lies between 1/2 and 1 and the bracket is (1/2, 1). Second bisection: q(3/4) = 243/1024 + 3/4 - 1 = -13/1024 < 0, so the bracket is (3/4, 1), of width 1/4. The true root is about 0.7549.
continuity-workshop.explain: Continuity is free because $q$ is a polynomial, and the opposite signs $q(0) = -1$, $q(1) = 1$ are the entire hypothesis. The instructive step is the second: $q(3/4) = -13/1024 \approx -0.0127$ is negative but only just, and a calculation rounded to two decimal places would report $0.00$ and destroy the bracket. Sign, not size, is what root bracketing consumes, so it must be determined exactly.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Prove that the equation $\cos x = x$ has a solution in the interval $(0,1)$. Construct a suitable function, justify its continuity from the continuity of its parts, apply the Intermediate Value Theorem explicitly, and state what your argument does not prove.
continuity-workshop.hint: Move everything to one side: let $h(x) = \cos x - x$ and hunt for a zero of $h$.
continuity-workshop.explain: Set $h(x) = \cos x - x$, continuous on $[0,1]$ as a difference of two continuous functions - this is exactly where the algebra of continuity earns its keep, since $h$ is not a polynomial and proving it continuous from the definition would be miserable. Then $h(0) = 1 > 0$ and $h(1) = \cos 1 - 1 \approx -0.4597 < 0$, so the Intermediate Value Theorem with $N = 0$ gives $c \in (0,1)$ with $h(c) = 0$, that is $\cos c = c$. What the argument does not prove is uniqueness, or where $c$ is; the true value is about $0.7391$, and the theorem supplied none of those digits.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Two students misuse the Intermediate Value Theorem. The first argues that since $f(x) = 1/x$ satisfies $f(-1) = -1$ and $f(1) = 1$, it must equal $0$ somewhere in $(-1,1)$. The second argues that since $\tan(\pi/4) = 1$ and $\tan(3\pi/4) = -1$, $\tan x$ must be zero somewhere in $(\pi/4, 3\pi/4)$. Explain precisely which hypothesis each has skipped and what actually happens on those intervals.
continuity-workshop.explain: Both have used the conclusion of a theorem whose hypothesis they never checked: continuity on the **whole closed interval**. $1/x$ has an infinite discontinuity at $0$, which sits inside $(-1,1)$, and it leaps from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ there without passing through any value at all; $\tan x$ has an infinite discontinuity at $\pi/2$, inside $(\pi/4, 3\pi/4)$, and is never zero on that interval. Sign changes are evidence of a root only for continuous functions - for everything else a sign change is just as easily the signature of a vertical asymptote.

continuity-workshop.prompt: Find every horizontal asymptote of $u(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{4x^2 + 1}}{3x - 5}$ and of $v(x) = \dfrac{5x - 2}{\sqrt{9x^2 + 4}}$, taking both $x \to \infty$ and $x \to -\infty$. Explain, using $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|$, why each function has two asymptotes rather than one.
continuity-workshop.answer: Write sqrt(4x^2 + 1) = |x| sqrt(4 + 1/x^2). As x -> +infinity, |x| = x, so u(x) -> x*2/(3x) = 2/3. As x -> -infinity, |x| = -x, so u(x) -> -2x/(3x) = -2/3. Hence u has horizontal asymptotes y = 2/3 and y = -2/3. Likewise sqrt(9x^2 + 4) = |x| sqrt(9 + 4/x^2), so v(x) -> 5x/(3x) = 5/3 as x -> +infinity and v(x) -> 5x/(-3x) = -5/3 as x -> -infinity, giving asymptotes y = 5/3 and y = -5/3. Two asymptotes appear because a square root is never negative while the linear part changes sign, so the quotient changes sign between the two ends.
continuity-workshop.hint: Pull $|x|$ out of the square root, then replace $|x|$ by $x$ or by $-x$ according to the direction you are travelling.
continuity-workshop.explain: $\sqrt{4x^2+1} = |x|\sqrt{4 + 1/x^2}$ behaves like $2|x|$, which is $2x$ on the right and $-2x$ on the left - so $u \to 2/3$ and $-2/3$, and $v \to 5/3$ and $-5/3$. The famous wrong answer is a single asymptote $y = 2/3$, produced by writing $\sqrt{4x^2} = 2x$ and forgetting the modulus. Degree counting alone cannot detect this, because degrees carry no sign information.

exam.prompt: By definition, $f$ is continuous at $a$ exactly when:
choices: $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists
$f(a)$ is defined and $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists
$f(a)$ is defined, $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, and the two are equal
$f$ is defined on some open interval containing $a$
exam.explain: All three clauses are needed, and the third is not implied by the first two: $f(x) = x^2$ for $x \neq 1$ with $f(1) = 5$ satisfies both of the others and is plainly discontinuous. Option $(1)$ describes a removable discontinuity just as happily as a continuous point, and option $(4)$ is a statement about the domain that says nothing about limits at all.

exam.prompt: By definition, the line $y = L$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f$ exactly when:
choices: $f(x) \neq L$ for all sufficiently large $x$
$\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L$ or $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L$
$\displaystyle\lim_{x \to L} f(x) = \infty$
the numerator and denominator of $f$ have the same degree
exam.explain: A horizontal asymptote is nothing but a finite limit in one of the two directions, and either direction suffices - which is why a function can have two of them. Option $(1)$ is the widespread belief that a graph may not touch its asymptote, and $\sin(x)/x$ crosses $y = 0$ infinitely often to refute it. Option $(3)$ describes a vertical asymptote, and option $(4)$ is a computational rule for one family of functions, not a definition.

exam.prompt: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2} & x \neq 2 \\ 7 & x = 2. \end{cases}$$ Give a number, then a clause number, then `removable`, `jump` or `infinite`, then a number.
exam.template:
the limit as x -> 2 is ___
the clause of continuity that fails is number ___
the discontinuity at x = 2 is ___
the single value of f(2) that repairs it is ___
exam.explain: Here $f(2) = 7$ exists and the limit is $4$, so clauses $(1)$ and $(2)$ both hold and only $(3)$ fails - the case that gets forgotten, because nothing is undefined and nothing blows up. It is removable, and the repair is $f(2) = 4$: you move the value to the limit, never the limit to the value, since redefining a function at one point cannot change any limit.

exam.prompt: Evaluate the end behaviour. Write fractions like `2/3` and whole numbers plainly; the last line wants two numbers.
exam.template:
(4x^3 - 2x)/(6x^3 + 5)    -> ___   as x -> oo
(x^2 + 1)/(x^3 - 2)       -> ___   as x -> oo
(6x^4 - x)/(2x^4 + 3x^2)  -> ___   as x -> oo
horizontal asymptotes of 3x/sqrt(x^2 + 1):  y = ___ and y = ___
exam.explain: The first and third have equal degrees, so the answers are $4/6 = 2/3$ and $6/2 = 3$ - lower-order terms are irrelevant however large their coefficients look. The second has a bigger denominator, so the limit is $0$. The last needs $\sqrt{x^2+1} = |x|\sqrt{1 + 1/x^2}$, giving $+3$ to the right and $-3$ to the left; answering with a single asymptote $y = 3$ is the standard casualty of writing $\sqrt{x^2} = x$.

exam.prompt: Order the steps of locating a root by the Intermediate Value Theorem and bisection.
fragments: Check that f is continuous on the whole closed interval [a, b] - a polynomial qualifies outright, a rational one only if no zero of its denominator lies inside.
Evaluate f(a) and f(b) and confirm that they have opposite signs.
Conclude from the Intermediate Value Theorem that f has at least one root in (a, b).
Evaluate f exactly at the midpoint m = (a + b)/2.
Keep whichever half still shows a sign change, and repeat to halve the uncertainty again.
exam.explain: Continuity is checked first because everything after it is invalid without it - a sign change across a vertical asymptote proves nothing whatever. The existence conclusion is drawn before any bisection, since bisection only narrows a root already known to be there; running the halvings on a function with a discontinuity converges perfectly happily onto the asymptote instead.

exam.prompt: Bracket a root of $g(x) = x^3 - x - 1$ on $[1,2]$. Write `negative` or `positive` for the signs, and write brackets exactly in the form `(1, 3/2)`.

steps.label: bracket after then testing the midpoint 5/4

exam.explain: $g(1) = -1$ and $g(2) = 5$, so the sign changes and a root exists in $(1,2)$. Since $g(3/2) = 7/8 > 0$, the sign change is now between $1$ and $3/2$, and you keep the half whose endpoints still disagree - keeping the half containing the larger value is the usual reflex and is exactly backwards. Then $g(5/4) = -19/64 < 0$ narrows it to $(5/4, 3/2)$, which contains the true root $1.3247\ldots$

exam.prompt: Find the value of $b$ making $$f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 + bx & x \le 2 \\ 3x + b & x > 2 \end{cases}$$ continuous at $x = 2$. Give the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and $f(2)$, and say why matching only the two formulas is enough here.
exam.answer: Both branches are polynomials, so each one-sided limit is a substitution. The left-hand limit is 4 + 2b, and since x = 2 belongs to the first branch, f(2) = 4 + 2b as well. The right-hand limit is 6 + b. Continuity requires 4 + 2b = 6 + b, so b = 2, and the common value is 4 + 4 = 8 = 6 + 2. Matching the two formulas suffices because f(2) is produced by one of those same formulas, so once the one-sided limits agree, clause (3) is satisfied automatically.
exam.hint: The $\le$ tells you which branch owns the point $x = 2$, and therefore which formula gives $f(2)$.
exam.explain: Substituting into each branch gives $4 + 2b$ on the left and $6 + b$ on the right, so $b = 2$ and both sides equal $8$. Clause $(3)$ needs no separate work only because $x = 2$ belongs to a branch that is itself continuous there - if the piecewise definition had assigned $f(2)$ some third value, matching the limits would have fixed clause $(2)$ and left a removable discontinuity behind.

exam.prompt: Give every interval on which $H(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x - 1}}{x - 4}$ is continuous, justifying each piece from the continuity rules for compositions and quotients. Say what happens at $x = 1$, what happens at $x = 4$, and why those two points fail for different reasons.
exam.answer: The numerator is the composition of the continuous square root with the polynomial x - 1, so it is defined and continuous wherever x - 1 >= 0, that is on [1, infinity). The denominator is a polynomial, continuous everywhere, and it vanishes only at x = 4. A quotient of continuous functions is continuous wherever the denominator is non-zero, so H is continuous on [1, 4) and on (4, infinity). At x = 1, H is continuous from the right only, because H is not defined at all for x < 1 - there is nothing to the left to check, so this is an endpoint, not a discontinuity. At x = 4 the numerator tends to sqrt(3) =/= 0 while the denominator tends to 0, so the limits are -infinity from the left and +infinity from the right: an infinite discontinuity with the vertical asymptote x = 4.
exam.hint: Two separate constraints: the square root needs $x \ge 1$, and the quotient needs $x \neq 4$.
exam.explain: The rules do all the work: composition gives continuity of $\sqrt{x-1}$ on $[1,\infty)$, and the quotient rule removes only $x = 4$, leaving $[1,4)$ and $(4,\infty)$. The distinction worth internalising is that $x = 1$ is an **endpoint** with one-sided continuity, not a discontinuity - a function cannot be discontinuous where it is not defined on either side - whereas $x = 4$ is a genuine infinite discontinuity sitting inside the domain's reach. Writing the answer as $(1,4) \cup (4,\infty)$ needlessly throws away the point $x = 1$, where $H(1) = 0/(-3) = 0$ is perfectly well behaved.

exam.prompt: Explain why the word **removable** is honest for one species of discontinuity, and why no redefinition of $f$ at a single point can ever remove a jump discontinuity. Use the fact that changing a function at one point changes none of its limits.
exam.explain: At a removable discontinuity the two sides already agree on a single finite $L$, so the only thing wrong is the value at the one point; setting $f(a) = L$ satisfies all three clauses at once. At a jump the two one-sided limits are different numbers, and altering $f$ at $a$ alone leaves both of them exactly as they were - limits are decided by the deleted neighbourhood, never by the point. Whatever value you nominate therefore disagrees with at least one side, so clause $(2)$ stays broken and no repair exists.

exam.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{7x^2 + 3}{2 - x^2}$, $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^2 + 1}{x^3 - 2}$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^3 + 1}{4x^2 - x}$. Then state every horizontal asymptote of each of the three functions, writing `none` where there is none, and justify each answer by degrees rather than by inspection.
exam.answer: First: numerator and denominator both have degree 2, so the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients, 7/(-1) = -7. The same holds as x -> -infinity, so y = -7 is the only horizontal asymptote. Second: degree 2 is less than degree 3, so dividing by x^3 gives (1/x + 1/x^3)/(1 - 2/x^3) -> 0. The same holds in the other direction, so y = 0 is the only horizontal asymptote. Third: degree 3 exceeds degree 2, so the quotient behaves like x/4 and tends to +infinity as x -> +infinity, and to -infinity as x -> -infinity. There is no horizontal asymptote at all: none.
exam.hint: Divide through by the highest power in the denominator each time, and read the leading coefficient of $2 - x^2$ carefully.
exam.explain: The answers are $-7$, $0$ and $+\infty$. The first is the classic trap: the leading coefficient of $2 - x^2$ is $-1$, not $2$, so the answer is $7/(-1) = -7$ and not $7/2$ - the constant term is irrelevant however prominently it is written. The third has no horizontal asymptote, because $\infty$ is not a number and an asymptote $y = L$ needs a real $L$; there is a slant asymptote instead, since the numerator wins by exactly one degree.

sections.title: From Average Speed to the Speed Right Now
sections.body:
Ask how fast a stone is moving over the whole of its flight and the question is easy: divide the height gained by the time taken. That number is an **average rate of change**, and geometrically it is the slope of the **secant** line joining two points of the graph, $$\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}.$$

Ask instead how fast the stone is moving **at the instant** $t = 1$ and the same recipe collapses. One instant is a single point, the height gained is $0$ and the time taken is $0$, and $\frac{0}{0}$ is not a number - it is the symptom of a question asked badly.

The repair is the whole of differential calculus in one move. Do not evaluate at the instant; evaluate on a short interval $[a, a+h]$, simplify the resulting **difference quotient** $\frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$ **while $h$ is still nonzero**, and only then let $h \to 0$. The algebra almost always cancels the offending $h$, leaving an expression that behaves perfectly well at $h = 0$.

So the instantaneous rate is not a quotient that we somehow evaluate at a point; it is the **limit of a family of honest quotients**. Nothing is ever divided by zero, and the geometry keeps pace: as $h \to 0$ the secant through $(a, f(a))$ and $(a+h, f(a+h))$ pivots about the fixed first point and settles onto the tangent.
sections.code:
A stone is thrown upward.  Its height in metres after t seconds:

    h(t) = 20t - 5t^2

AVERAGE velocity over [1, 1 + dt] is the slope of a SECANT line:

    h(1)      = 20 - 5                    = 15
    h(1 + dt) = 20(1 + dt) - 5(1 + dt)^2
              = 20 + 20dt - 5 - 10dt - 5dt^2
              = 15 + 10dt - 5dt^2

    average   = ( h(1 + dt) - h(1) ) / dt
              = ( 10dt - 5dt^2 ) / dt
              = 10 - 5dt            <- true for EVERY dt =/= 0

Now shrink the interval.  dt is never allowed to BE zero, but it is
allowed to be sent to zero:

    dt = 1      ->  10 - 5      =  5     m/s
    dt = 0.1    ->  10 - 0.5    =  9.5   m/s
    dt = 0.01   ->  10 - 0.05   =  9.95  m/s
    dt -> 0     ->  10                   m/s   <- the INSTANT

The cancellation is the trick, and the only trick.  It converts an
expression that reads 0/0 at dt = 0 into one, 10 - 5dt, that is
perfectly comfortable there.  So h'(1) = 10 m/s.

annotations.text: Everything after the first term is a multiple of dt. That is not luck: h(1 + dt) must reduce to h(1) when dt = 0, so the difference is forced to carry a factor of dt.
Read the arrow as a warning. The simplified form equals the quotient only where the quotient exists; at dt = 0 the left-hand side is undefined while the right-hand side is 10.
The numbers are converging on 10, but a table can never prove a limit - it can only suggest one. The algebra above is the proof.
This is the pattern for every derivative on this floor: expand, find the common factor of h, cancel it, then substitute h = 0 into what survives.

checkpoint.prompt: For the stone $h(t) = 20t - 5t^2$, the average velocity over $[1, 1+\Delta t]$ simplifies to $10 - 5\,\Delta t$. Give each value as a plain number.
checkpoint.template:
average velocity over [1, 1.2] = ___ m/s
average velocity over [1, 1.02] = ___ m/s
instantaneous velocity at t = 1 = ___ m/s
checkpoint.explain: Substituting $\Delta t = 0.2$ and $\Delta t = 0.02$ into $10 - 5\,\Delta t$ gives $9$ and $9.9$, and the limit as $\Delta t \to 0$ gives $10$. Note that no average equals $10$ for any interval of positive length: the instantaneous value is a limit the averages approach, never one of them. Reading the last blank off the table rather than off the algebra is the habit to break early.

sections.title: The Definition, the Ritual, and the Notation
sections.body:
The **derivative of $f$ at $a$** is that limit, given a name: $$f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h},$$ and $f$ is called **differentiable at $a$** when this limit exists as a finite number. Substituting $x = a + h$ gives the equivalent form $f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$; the two say the same thing, and the first is usually easier to expand while the second is usually easier to factorise.

Computing one is a fixed four-step ritual: write the quotient, expand the numerator, cancel the factor of $h$ that always appears, then substitute $h = 0$. The cancellation is legal precisely because $h \neq 0$ throughout - a limit as $h \to 0$ never asks what happens **at** $0$.

Letting $a$ vary turns the derivative into a new function $f'$, whose domain is the set of points where the limit exists and may be smaller than the domain of $f$. That shift - from a number attached to one point to a function defined on a set - is what makes the rest of the subject possible.

Three notations coexist. Lagrange's $f'(x)$ names the derived function and $f'(a)$ evaluates it; Leibniz's $\frac{dy}{dx}$ remembers that the derivative grew out of a genuine quotient $\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ of real differences, while $\frac{dy}{dx}\Big|_{x=a}$ pins down the point and $\frac{d}{dx}f(x)$ names the operation. Leibniz's symbol is a single indivisible piece of notation and not a fraction of two numbers - but it is deliberately shaped like one, because it records where the limit came from and it keeps the units honest.
sections.code:
DEFINITION      f'(a) = lim   ( f(a + h) - f(a) ) / h
                        h->0

EXAMPLE 1   f(x) = 1/x   at a = 2

   ( 1/(2+h) - 1/2 ) / h  =  ( (2 - (2+h)) / (2(2+h)) ) / h     common denominator
                          =  ( -h / (2(2+h)) ) / h
                          =  -1 / (2(2+h))                      the h cancels
   h -> 0                 =  -1/4                               so f'(2) = -1/4

EXAMPLE 2   f(x) = sqrt(x)   at a = 4        multiply by the conjugate

   ( sqrt(4+h) - 2 ) / h  =  ( sqrt(4+h) - 2 )( sqrt(4+h) + 2 )
                             ---------------------------------
                                    h ( sqrt(4+h) + 2 )
                          =  ( (4 + h) - 4 ) / ( h ( sqrt(4+h) + 2 ) )
                          =  1 / ( sqrt(4+h) + 2 )
   h -> 0                 =  1/4                                so f'(4) = 1/4

EXAMPLE 3   f(x) = x^3     at a general x    -> the derivative FUNCTION

   ( (x+h)^3 - x^3 ) / h  =  ( 3x^2 h + 3x h^2 + h^3 ) / h
                          =  3x^2 + 3xh + h^2
   h -> 0                 =  3x^2                               so f'(x) = 3x^2

NOTATION      f'(x)      Lagrange, the derived function
              dy/dx      Leibniz, from  (delta y)/(delta x)
              dy/dx|x=a  the derivative evaluated at a
              d/dx f(x)  'differentiate this' as an operation

annotations.text: Rational functions need one common denominator before anything can cancel. Subtracting first and dividing by h second keeps the algebra from sprawling.
A difference of square roots hides its factor of h until the conjugate exposes it. This one manoeuvre handles every root you will meet from the definition.
Every surviving term either has no h - that is the answer - or has a factor of h and therefore dies. Sorting terms that way makes the limit a glance rather than a calculation.
If y is metres and x is seconds, dy/dx carries metres per second. Leibniz's notation is the only one of the three that displays its own units.

checkpoint.prompt: Use the definition to compute $f'(3)$ for $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$. Show the common denominator, the cancellation of $h$, and the substitution $h = 0$.
checkpoint.answer: (1/(3+h) - 1/3)/h = ((3 - (3+h))/(3(3+h)))/h = (-h/(3(3+h)))/h = -1/(3(3+h)). Letting h -> 0 gives f'(3) = -1/9. The tangent to y = 1/x at (3, 1/3) therefore has slope -1/9, negative because 1/x is decreasing there.
checkpoint.explain: Combining over the common denominator $3(3+h)$ turns the numerator into $-h$, so dividing by $h$ leaves $\frac{-1}{3(3+h)}$, which is a perfectly ordinary expression at $h = 0$ and evaluates to $-\frac{1}{9}$. The famous wrong answer is $+\frac{1}{9}$: the sign is easy to lose, though $\frac{1}{3+h} < \frac{1}{3}$ guarantees the numerator was always going to be negative. A second common slip is reading $-\frac{1}{3^2}$ as $-\frac{1}{6}$, confusing the square with a doubling.

sections.title: The Tangent Line as a Local Linear Approximation
sections.body:
A tangent line is often described as a line touching the curve at one point, which is wrong twice over: the tangent to $y = x^3$ at the origin crosses the curve, and a line can meet a curve at exactly one point without being tangent to anything. The honest definition is the limiting one - the **tangent line at $a$** is the line through $(a, f(a))$ whose slope is $f'(a)$, the limit of the secant slopes.

Written out, that line is $$L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)\,(x - a).$$ It is the unique line agreeing with $f$ in **value** and in **slope** at $a$, which is why it is also called the **linear approximation** or **linearisation** of $f$ near $a$: among all lines it is the one whose error dies fastest as $x \to a$.

That gives the derivative a practical face. Near $a$ a differentiable function is **indistinguishable from a straight line** at small enough scale - zoom far enough into a smooth graph and it flattens onto its tangent. This is **local linearity**, and it is what differentiability really means geometrically.

The approximation is local, and the error grows with distance and with curvature. Where the graph bends downwards the tangent lies above it and $L(x)$ overestimates; where it bends upwards the tangent lies below and $L(x)$ underestimates. Using the linearisation far from $a$ is the standard way to obtain a plausible and badly wrong number.
sections.code:
f(x) = sqrt(x)      at a = 4:   f(4) = 2,   f'(4) = 1/4

TANGENT LINE      L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)
                       = 2 + (1/4)(x - 4)
